analysis.one_liner: Repeals special tax breaks for large oil companies and adds a new excise tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2010 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died without a vote when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take away several tax breaks available only to oil and gas companies — the ability to immediately deduct drilling costs, a depletion allowance, a deduction for domestic production income, and a foreign tax credit trick that lets big oil companies treat payments to foreign governments as tax payments. It would also impose a new 13 percent tax on oil and gas produced from federal waters in the Gulf of Mexico, with a credit for royalties already paid. Only companies with more than $100 million in gross revenues would be affected. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the beneficiaries would have been the U.S. Treasury and taxpayers generally, through higher revenue from the five largest oil companies' repealed deductions and the new Gulf excise tax, plus small oil and gas producers (under $100 million in gross revenues), who would keep every preference the big companies lose and gain a competitive edge. Gulf Coast residents and taxpayers who might otherwise bear more spill-related and cleanup costs would also benefit from a tax tied directly to offshore production.

how_it_helps.text: It removes five tax preferences available only to oil and gas producers — immediate expensing of drilling costs, a deduction for tertiary injectants, a passive-loss exception, percentage depletion, and a domestic manufacturing deduction — for companies with over $100 million in gross revenues.
It imposes a 13 percent excise tax on oil and gas removed from federal lands on the Outer Continental Shelf in the Gulf of Mexico, with a credit for federal royalties already paid.

It closes the 'dual capacity' foreign tax credit that lets the largest integrated oil companies count payments to foreign governments as income taxes even when those payments are really royalties for access to oil fields.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on large oil and gas companies — those above $100 million in gross revenues and the biggest integrated producers — which would lose billions in deductions and pay a new 13 percent tax on Gulf offshore production. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through fuel prices, and the industry argued the changes would discourage domestic drilling investment.

drawbacks.text: The new 13 percent excise tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production was a stiff new levy on top of existing royalties, and producers could pass higher costs through to consumers at the pump.

Repealing intangible drilling cost expensing and stretching geological survey costs over seven years raises the upfront cost of exploration, which the industry argued would reduce domestic drilling activity and domestic production.

The bill left the revenue's purpose unstated in its text — unlike companion versions of this proposal in 2010, it did not earmark proceeds for anything such as spill response or deficit reduction, making it a pure tax increase on the industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was more tax revenue from the largest and most profitable oil companies and a level playing field between big producers and smaller ones; the cost, as the industry argued in debates over similar proposals, was the risk of somewhat less domestic drilling investment and possibly modestly higher prices. On the merits the bill was a targeted removal of special tax breaks, not an industry-wide tax increase, though the 13 percent Gulf excise tax was a heavier lift and its revenue purpose went unstated in the bill text. The bigger weakness is what never happened: no committee held it to account, so the public never learned whether its estimates held up.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never considered it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced S. 3405 on May 24, 2010, with Senator Nelson of Florida and Senator Merkley as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill ended with only 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 100 senators.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies are better off: the deductions, depletion allowance, foreign tax credit treatment, and the new Gulf excise tax all went away with the bill, and none of those provisions has been locked in by this outcome — they simply remain available.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal oil and gas tax preferences and add a Gulf of Mexico excise tax.

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson of Florida and Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining eight months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no party split can be measured; all four cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill strips the industry's dedicated tax deductions, percentage depletion, the domestic manufacturing deduction, and a foreign tax credit trick, and adds a 13 percent excise tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production for companies above $100 million in gross revenues. Smaller producers are spared, so the cost falls entirely on the largest companies.

industries.industry: Small and independent oil and gas operators
industries.note: The $100 million gross-revenue threshold exempts smaller producers from every provision, so they keep all the tax preferences the big companies would lose — a relative competitive advantage at no cost to them.
